result.summary: After burying Tiphys, the Argonauts take heart from Ancaeus, who becomes helmsman, and sail east along the Black Sea coast, passing legendary sites and the Amazons. They drive off the birds of Ares, rescue the shipwrecked sons of Phrixus, who are kin to Jason, and with them reach the river Phasis in Colchis.

scenes.title: Tiphys dies; Ancaeus takes the helm
scenes.summary: Tiphys dies and is buried. The crew despair until Hera inspires Ancaeus, and Peleus rallies them. Ancaeus is chosen as steersman.
scenes.stakes: The expedition may be abandoned, leaving the crew to grow old in a strange land.

place.name: Land of the Mariandyni, by the Acheron

scenes.title: Sailing past Sthenelus's tomb to Sinope
scenes.summary: They sail past the Callichorus and halt at the tomb of Sthenelus, whose ghost appears. They then sail on to Sinope, where the sons of Deimachus join them, and pass the Halys.

scenes.title: Amazons, Chalybes and strange peoples
scenes.summary: They shelter at the Thermodon and escape a fight with the Amazons. They then pass the Chalybes, Tibareni and Mossynoeci, whose customs are described.
scenes.stakes: A battle with the fierce Amazons is narrowly avoided.

scenes.title: The birds of Ares
scenes.summary: Birds of the island of Ares wound Oileus. Amphidamas advises scaring them with noise and a roof of shields, and the trick works.
scenes.stakes: Arrow-like feathers from the birds threaten the crew as they land.

scenes.title: Shipwreck of Phrixus's sons
scenes.summary: The narrator explains that the sons of Phrixus were wrecked in a storm sent by Zeus and cast ashore on the island.
scenes.stakes: The sons of Phrixus are nearly drowned.

scenes.title: Meeting kin and warnings of Aeetes
scenes.summary: Argus tells his story, and Jason reveals they are kin and gives clothes. After a sacrifice at the temple of Ares, Argus warns of Aeetes and the serpent, and Peleus reassures them.
scenes.stakes: Fear that Aeetes and the guardian serpent make the quest deadly.

place.name: Temple of Ares on the island

scenes.title: Past Prometheus to the Phasis
scenes.summary: They pass Philyra's island, see Prometheus and his eagle, and enter the Phasis. Jason pours libations and they anchor in a backwater.
scenes.stakes: They arrive in hostile Colchis, where Aeetes may refuse the fleece.

alias_notes.explanation: epithet for Dionysus, who is not named in this translation here

notable_quotes.reason: Argus's plea invoking Zeus as protector of suppliants and strangers, the theme of guest-friendship.
Memorable hawk simile for the Argo's smooth flight.
Vivid simile of shields locked like roof tiles.

analysis.text: Loss of the helmsman and seer tests the crew's resolve, and divine aid via Hera and Athena's ship keeps the quest alive. Hospitality and kinship, shown in the rescue of Phrixus's sons, drive the plot.
The voyage along the Black Sea coast reflects Greek geographical lore and colonial knowledge of Pontic peoples, with ethnographic digressions on customs such as the Tibareni's couvade.

legacy.text: The shield-and-noise trick against the birds echoes the Stymphalian birds of Heracles and the Roman testudo shield formation.

fun_facts.text: Apollonius's description of the Tibareni men lying in bed at childbirth is an early account of couvade, a custom later recorded in many cultures.

language_notes.text: The first barrow was raised for Idmon, the seer killed by a boar; Tiphys is now the second comrade buried on this shore.
The 'son of Abas' is Idmon the seer, whose burial has just taken place; Tiphys is laid beside him.
Parthenia was an earlier home of Ancaeus, on Samos; he says Jason chose him for his skill with ships, not fighting.
'Bootless' means useless or without profit; the grief achieves nothing.
'Fell' means cruel or terrible; 'enshroud' here means wrap in or cover over.
The Nysean son of Zeus is Dionysus, god of wine, who in myth returned from India and danced with his followers; Callichorus means 'fair dances'.
A barrow is a burial mound raised over a tomb.
The ghost 'craved to behold men' because the dead long to see the living; Persephone, queen of the dead, lets it rise briefly.
Propitiate means to appease the ghost with libations, offerings of wine or other liquid poured out.
Sheets are ropes controlling the lower corners of the sail; making it taut to both sheets means trimming it to catch the wind.
The maid, daughter of Leto, is Artemis, goddess of the hunt, who bathes after hunting.
Zeus tricked by his own promise: he swore to grant Sinope any wish, and she asked to stay a virgin.
Refers to Heracles' ninth labour, fetching the Amazon queen's girdle. Here the girdle is given as ransom for Melanippe, Hippolyte's sister.
Pontus means the sea, here the Black Sea (the Euxine).
The sentence is muddled: 'would have fought... had not the breezes of Argestes come' means a fair west-north-west wind rose and prevented the battle.
'Exchange their wages for daily sustenance' means they sell their iron-work to buy food, since they do not farm.
Describes couvade, a custom in which the father imitates childbirth while the mother recovers; reported of several ancient peoples.
'Poor wretch!' is the narrator's aside, pitying the king for the harsh penalty that follows if he judges wrongly.
"Cleft their way with oars" means they cut through the water by rowing; the breeze that had helped them failed at dusk.
"I trow" is archaic for "I believe" or "I think"; "avail" means help or be of use.
Phineus, the blind seer, had told the Argonauts they must land on the island of Ares; they are bound by his instructions.
Heracles drove off the man-eating Stymphalian birds in Arcadia as one of his labours; here he is a former comrade of the Argonauts.
A rattle of bronze was a noisemaker; Heracles scared the birds by clattering it rather than by shooting.
"The son of Cronos" is Jove (the Greek Zeus), god of the sky and storms, here sending hail.
Phrixus fled Greece on a golden ram and died in Colchis, leaving wealth at Orchomenus; his sons now go to claim it.
Arcturus is a star whose rising was linked with stormy weather; the wind and rain are said to mark its path.
"Zeus the Beholder" invokes Zeus as the god who watches over suppliants and sees how strangers are treated.
"I trow" is archaic for "I believe"; "Aeolid" means descendant of Aeolus.
"I ween" is archaic for "I think"; "sore" means grievous.
The Amazons, a warlike nation of women, were associated with Ares; this island shrine was their place of worship.
Phrixus was rescued from a murderous step-mother (Ino) and from sacrifice by the golden ram, which Jason recalls as Zeus's saving act.
The clashing rocks are the Symplegades, which crushed ships passing through the Bosporus; the Argo has already survived them.
Typhaon (Typhon) was a monster who challenged Zeus and was struck down by his thunderbolt; the serpent's birth is tied to this myth.
Cronos hid his affair from his wife Rhea by becoming a horse; Cheiron, the wise centaur, was the result. Zeus was hidden in Crete from his father Cronos.
The Curetes were divine attendants who guarded the infant Zeus, clashing weapons to drown his cries; "dalliance" means amorous play.
Prometheus was chained for stealing fire from the gods for humankind; his liver, regrowing daily, was eaten by Zeus's eagle.
"Galling fetters" means chafing, painful chains.
"Bourne" means boundary or limit; the Phasis marks the far edge of their voyage.
The "mast-crutch" is a forked support on which the lowered mast and furled sail rested.
The fleece guarded by the serpent is the Golden Fleece, the goal of the voyage.
"Welcome their ship's hawsers" means accept the mooring cables kindly, that is, grant a safe landing.

context_notes.text: Tiphys was the Argo's helmsman, famed for steering skill. His death leaves the ship without a pilot.
Hera favours Jason and the expedition throughout the poem, and often steps in to inspire or protect the crew.
Peleus, son of Aeacus, is one of the Argonauts and later the father of Achilles.
Sthenelus joined Heracles' expedition against the Amazons and died of a wound on the return; he is the son of Actor.
Apollo was invoked as protector of sailors; the offerings thank him and seek safe passage. Lyra is Greek for lyre.
These three brothers from Tricca in Thessaly had been separated from Heracles earlier on the voyage and now rejoin the heroes.
Ares was the Greek god of war, and the Amazons were a warrior people of women, said to descend from him.
The Thermodon is a river on the Black Sea coast of Asia Minor, traditionally the homeland of the Amazons.
The Chalybes were famed ancient ironworkers on the south coast of the Black Sea.
The Mossynoeci's name is linked to the Greek word mossyn, a wooden tower or hut, which is the derivation the poem alludes to.
The birds of Ares were sacred to the war god and, in this tradition, could shoot feathers like arrows at intruders.
Eribotes and Clytius are among the Argonauts; Clytius is a skilled archer, son of Eurytus.
Half the crew keep rowing while the others form a defensive cover, so the ship keeps moving under attack.
Phineus, the blind prophet, had told the Argonauts they would meet help on this island, so Jason recognizes the sons of Phrixus as that help.
Jason is descended from Cretheus, brother of Athamas, so Phrixus's sons, being Athamas's grandsons, are his cousins.
Helios is the sun god; Aeetes' claim to be his son shows his pride and power.
The Caucasus was imagined as the edge of the known world, a fitting place for Prometheus's punishment.
Aea, city of King Aeetes, is the Colchian destination where Jason must win the fleece.
Libations, poured offerings of wine and honey, were customary to honor local gods and the dead on arriving in a new land.

literary_notes.text: The narrator's opening question draws attention to the next death and carries the story forward.
The silent, cloaked men sprawled on the shore and refusing food vividly convey their despair.
Jason's gloomy, fatalistic speech shows him as often despondent, in contrast with the practical Ancaeus and Peleus.
The vivid picture of the ghost's four-peaked helm and blood-red crest makes the apparition seem solid and martial.
The ship's smooth, steady speed is compared to a hawk poised on outspread wings, conveying effortless motion.
Sinope's cleverness turns the gods' own desire and promises against them, so the powerful are outwitted by a maiden.
The river's 'arching crest of foam' bursting into the sea gives the water a living, charging force, after the long image of winding streams.
The Mossynoeci reverse normal Greek conduct, public and private swapped, which makes them vividly alien and shows the poem's ethnographic curiosity.
Comparing them to herding swine expresses the narrator's Greek disgust and marks them as barbaric.
The shields locked over the ship are compared to tiles on a roof, which shows the tight, protective covering.
The crew's shout is likened to the roar of armies clashing, making their cry seem like a battle sound.
The hailstorm and prepared householders parallel the feather shower and the sheltered heroes; the final clause completes the comparison.
The north wind is given purpose and moods, gentle by day and raging by night, acting as Zeus's agent.
The theme of Zeus guarding suppliants and strangers (xenia) recurs, framing hospitality as a sacred duty.
Jason says Zeus protects the god-fearing and just, though the Argonauts' own quest involves taking the fleece by force if necessary.
The sleepless serpent and Aeetes' strength hint at the dangers awaiting the heroes in Colchis.
Pale cheeks show the crew's fear in a single vivid image.
The repeated "And lo" and the opened gulf and rising crags give a sudden, dramatic vision of Prometheus's torment.
The eagle's wings fan all the sails from high above, stressing its supernatural size.
The eagle's wing-feathers are compared to polished oars, making its enormous size and steady, rowing motion vivid to sailors.
